era_visual_canon.clothing: Mid-20th-century working-class Australian outback dress. Miners and mill workers wear khaki or grey cotton work shirts, sturdy trousers or overalls, heavy leather boots, soft caps or felt hats, and are often coated in pale dust; no respirators in the early decades, only basic cloth masks at most. Women wear modest cotton day dresses or blouses with skirts and cardigans, with practical shoes. Children wear simple cotton shorts, shirts and dresses. Officials wear shirts and ties, trousers, and sometimes jackets and hats. Later eras (1980s-2020s) shift to plain casual wear for residents and legal or media figures.
era_visual_canon.technology: Mid-century analog technology: film cameras, black-and-white and early color photography, paper files and typewritten reports, carbon-copy memos, wired telephones, radio, mechanical dust-sampling instruments, hand-held ledgers, and later 1980s video interviews and office computers. Dust-reduction equipment appears only from the late 1950s. NO smartphones, NO digital displays, NO drones, NO GPS screens in the 1937-1966 period.
era_visual_canon.vehicles_machinery: Small propeller aircraft landing on a bare airstrip, 1940s-1960s trucks and utility vehicles, tipper trucks dumping tailings, dusty sedans and station wagons, ore-crushing and milling machinery with open conveyors and chutes, ventilation and dust-extraction hoods from the late 1950s, bulldozers and earth-moving plant for demolition in the late 1980s-1990s. Ocean liners are used for migrant voyages via the Suez Canal.
era_visual_canon.interiors: Modest company housing of corrugated metal, timber and asbestos-cement (uralita) sheeting, with plain furnishings, fine dust settling on surfaces, simple kitchens and bedrooms. Dusty mill interiors with machinery and a thick suspended dust cloud. A small hospital, a school, a church and a police station with plain 1960s institutional fittings. Later interiors show gutted, empty or demolished buildings.
era_visual_canon.forbidden_anachronisms: Smartphones, flat-screen displays, modern high-visibility safety gear and modern respirators on 1937-1966 workers, 21st-century cars, modern tourist infrastructure or signage in the town, drones, solar panels, modern branded logos, tidy clean surfaces without fiber dust, and living residents shown after the 2022-2023 evacuation.
era_visual_canon.materials_textures: Crumbly, fibrous blue asbestos tailings spread as loose gravel-like surfacing over roads, yards, schoolyards, public spaces and the airstrip, which shed fine powder when touched. Corrugated sheet metal, timber and uralita (asbestos-cement) cladding on buildings. Dry, powdery desert ground. Fibers can be teased apart by hand. Fine dust coats workers, machinery and surfaces around the mill.
era_visual_canon.color_palette: red desert earth and rust-brown ground, pale grey-blue tailings surfacing, dull silver-grey corrugated metal, weathered timber and pale dusty grey-white coating on mill surfaces, with sepia tones in surviving family photographs.
era_visual_canon.scale_dimensions: Remote Pilbara gorge town served by a small-aircraft airstrip. Three mines produced about 150,000 tonnes of commercial asbestos in 1937-1966, leaving over three million tonnes of tailings. The current Wittenoom Asbestos Management Area covers 46,840 hectares. Individual building dimensions are not documented in the sources.
era_visual_canon.distinctive_features: A small desert town in the red Pilbara gorges whose roads, yards, schoolyards and airstrip were surfaced with grey-blue asbestos tailings, with a dust cloud hanging over the mill. Later it becomes an emptied, barricaded ghost town with no standing structures.
era_visual_canon.demographics: Mostly male miners and mill workers, including post-war displaced persons assigned by the federal government and European recruits, among them Spanish migrant families (couples, young children and babies) arriving from 1962. Management, officials and inspectors are Australian and company staff. Banjima traditional owners are the Country's custodians. Workers wear dust-covered work clothes; families wear modest cotton clothing.
era_visual_canon.visual_reference_availability: VISUAL SOURCES: surviving family photographs (sepia family photos, a family portrait with a bandaged foot, a photo tied to a baptism dated 7 July 1963) and interview footage of survivors. TEXT SOURCES (not photographic in this pool): descriptions of tailings surfacing, uralita and corrugated housing, dust clouds at the mill, red earth around the airstrip, and children playing with asbestos, all drawn from testimony and official reports. Exact building shapes, layouts and dimensions are INFERENCE and not documented here. Ethnicity and clothing of groups come from the written record, not photographs.

condition_evolution.at_event: Operating company town (1937-1966): dusty, occupied streets, yards and schoolyards surfaced with blue-grey tailings, houses of corrugated metal, timber and uralita, a mill shrouded in a thick dust cloud, a working airstrip and workers covered in fine pale dust.
condition_evolution.later: Progressive decline after mining ended in December 1966: from 1978 the state reduced the town, and buildings were demolished and services (school, nursing post, police station) closed in 1986-1992. The airport closed in 1993, the power grid was disconnected in 2006, and the town was abolished and erased from maps and signs in 2007. The last residents left in 2022-2023, and final demolition of the structures was reported in 2022-2023 (sources disagree on the year). Today the site is an emptied, barricaded, contaminated ghost town, with asbestos spread by wind and water down the creeks toward the Fortescue.

periods.clothing: Prospectors and early miners in rugged khaki work shirts, trousers, boots and wide-brimmed felt hats; officials in suits or shirts with ties and hats.
periods.technology: Hand tools, manual sampling, typed reports, paper correspondence, radio and wired telephone. NO digital technology, NO modern respirators.
periods.vehicles_machinery: 1930s-1940s trucks, early crushing and milling plant, rough gorge tracks, small aircraft for access.
periods.interiors: Basic bush huts, tin and timber sheds, simple mine offices with timber desks and paper files.

periods.clothing: Dusty work shirts, overalls and boots for male workers; migrant families in modest 1950s-60s cotton dresses, shirts, knitwear and plain shoes; officials in shirts and ties.
periods.technology: Film photography, typewriters, reel-to-reel and early radio equipment, dust-extraction hoods, mechanical industrial machinery. NO LED screens, NO digital devices.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Small propeller aircraft, tipper trucks dumping tailings, utility vehicles, working mill machinery, ocean liner voyages for migrants.
periods.interiors: Company houses of corrugated metal, timber and uralita; a dusty mill with a thick suspended dust cloud; a small hospital, a school and a church.

periods.clothing: Plain 1970s-80s casual clothing for the remaining residents; suits and ties for lawyers, judges and officials; work clothes and hard hats for demolition crews.
periods.technology: Photocopied reports, television and film cameras, wired phones, early office computers by the late 1980s. NO smartphones, NO tablets.
periods.vehicles_machinery: 1970s-80s sedans and utility vehicles, bulldozers and demolition equipment, trucks.
periods.interiors: Shrinking town with emptied houses, closing school, clinic and police station, and court and parliamentary hearing rooms with 1980s institutional decor.

periods.clothing: Contemporary but plain dress for officials, legal figures and elders in documentary settings; protective white suits, if shown, only for official modern site visits.
periods.technology: Contemporary reports, video interviews, environmental sampling, legal filings. Modern devices appear only in present-day framing and never inside 1937-1966 scenes.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Modern four-wheel-drive vehicles and permanent road barricades at the town and gorge entrances.
periods.interiors: Emptied, demolished or overgrown townsite, with barricaded entrances and no inhabited interiors; offices and courts appear only in a modern legal or political context.
